paras: The killing of Henry Gilbreath was the fatal shooting of a Black private of the 366th Infantry by Patrolman Crump in Chattanooga, Tennessee, early on a Thursday morning in late March 1919. Crump said he fired as the soldier came at him with a knife, and a coroner's jury and an army board of officers arranged a joint inquiry into the death.

According to the only report found, Crump shot and killed Gilbreath, described as "a negro soldier of the 366th Infantry," early on Thursday morning, most likely March 27. Crump's account was that he shot Gilbreath "while the latter was advancing with a knife following a mix-up of the two men." No other version of the encounter, from witnesses or from the soldier's side, appears in the coverage.

The jury of view appointed by Coroner O'Donohue and a board of officers from Fort Oglethorpe scheduled a joint investigation of the death for 3:30 in the afternoon. Counsel for both the state and the defense were expected to attend the hearing. The coroner's jury was made up of O. K. LeBron, Henry Hart, Cal Sterchi, Hal F. Wiltse, W. H. Ford, Terrel Clemons and J. F. Burkhart. No report of the inquiry's finding, of any charge against Crump, or of a trial was found.

The Ohio State Monitor carried the story on its front page on March 29, 1919, under the headline "INVESTIGATION TODAY OF NEGRO SOLDIER KILLING." The item was datelined "Chatt., Tenn" and read like a reprinted local report, speaking of the hearing as taking place "this afternoon." It gave the patrolman's knife story as something Crump "claims" rather than as fact, and it added no editorial comment. No other Black newspaper report of the shooting was found.

reader.title: Killing of Henry Gilbreath
bases: A single city patrolman, Crump, shot and killed a Black soldier after what he called a mix-up between the two men; no crowd or mob is mentioned (A1).
Only one brief Black-press item (A1) reports the killing; no second independent report was found in the Black press.
